title: Lending Solutions Redesign
subtitle: Reinventing end-to-end lending for J.P. Morgan Private Bank — and proving it worked by building the validation loop myself.

meta.label: Company
meta.value: J.P. Morgan Private Bank, Wealth Management

meta.label: Team
meta.value: Product (multi-domain POs), Engineering, UX Research, Credit Middle Office

indexedSections.title: A private bank running on disconnected tools

value: J.P. Morgan Private Bank serves ultra-high-net-worth clients across 140+ countries with lending products like Securities-Based Lending and Custom Credit.

But behind every loan sat a broken workflow. A single request meant jumping between disconnected applications — re-keying data, chasing manual handoffs with Credit Middle Officers, and relying on institutional memory.
I owned the end-to-end lending redesign, across two surfaces.

items.title: Loan Request App 3.0
items.desc: The origination surface where Advisors submit SBL, Custom Credit, and PLP tickets — new deals and amendments — across USPB, EMEA, APAC, and LatAm.

items.title: Lending Workspace
items.desc: The hub bringing every Private Bank lending tool under one roof.

blocks.label: Lending Workspace — deal journey, prospects, portfolio health, and insights in one place
The gap
blocks.value: The tools existed. The experience didn't.

indexedSections.title: People with no room for internal friction

blocks.value: My primary users were Advisors and Bankers serving UHNW clients who expect fast answers.

items.title: Time-starved
items.desc: Every client minute is high-stakes. Tooling friction is a direct tax on client service.

items.title: High-consequence
items.desc: A single ticket can move eight figures. An error isn't an inconvenience, it's a risk event.

items.title: Knowledge-gated
items.desc: Complex, multi-step, tool-dependent workflows that punished anyone without deep institutional knowledge.

blocks.label: Two primary users — ~500 Client Advisors and ~900 Bankers across the Private Bank
Design principle
blocks.value: Remove the friction that wastes time. Keep the friction that protects the client.

indexedSections.title: A variable matrix, not a form

value: The v1 experience was a flat, linear form: no conditional logic, no real-time feedback, no guidance. Advisors were expected to already know what to fill in, when, and why.
But a loan request isn't a form — it's a combinatorial matrix.

blocks.label: What the old flow cost — NIGO returns, mid-flow restarts, and manual CMO handoffs

blocks.value: That explodes into hundreds of states. Two problems compounded it.

items.label: Problem A
items.title: No single source of truth
items.desc: Each domain had its own Product Owner with limited cross-domain visibility — producing conflicting requirements, overlapping asks, and three months of circular debate over whose process was standard.

items.label: Problem B
items.title: No shared mental model
items.desc: Everyone pictured the lending space differently, so we argued about fields when the disagreement was structural.

blocks.title: Map the whole space before touching a screen

value: Instead of designing screens, I built an information architecture covering every domain, product, and region — one holistic view of the entire lending surface.
The IA's value wasn't aesthetic. It turned invisible disagreements into pointable nodes. “Whose process wins?” became “which region owns this node?” — a solvable question.
I designed the space first, then the screens, so every later decision had a home.

blocks.label: Information architecture — the full Lending Workspace surface

blocks.title: Unify the skeleton, localize the organs

blocks.value: The hardest tension surfaced immediately: how much to unify?

items.label: Fully global
items.desc: EMEA's mandatory compliance fields get cut. A non-negotiable red line.

items.label: Fully local
items.desc: We're back to four disconnected tools. Unification dies.

blocks.value: My decision: one shared flow, navigation, and mental model across all regions, with conditional logic injecting region-specific fields and disclosures inside each step. Advisors experience one product; the system adapts underneath.

blocks.label: One skeleton, regional organs — the same flow across EMEA, APAC, LatAm, and USPB

blocks.title: Lead by showing — a prototype that ended the debate

value: I could say “skeleton vs. organs,” but POs didn't buy abstractions — they kept asking “is my field still there?”

So I stopped arguing and built an interactive prototype with LLM-assisted tooling. Select EMEA and the three compliance fields appear. Switch to USPB and they disappear — the rest of the flow doesn't move.

blocks.value: Oh — my field wasn't deleted. It just doesn't exist in other regions.

value: Three months of debate collapsed in a fifteen-minute walkthrough.
When consensus is missing and talk won't converge, a prototype isn't a deliverable — it's a decision instrument. It swaps “who's right” for “does this work.”

blocks.label: The debate, in artifact form — every stakeholder's “is my field still there?” annotated on one screen

blocks.title: The friction I chose to keep

blocks.value: My first pass optimized for pure speed — auto-advancing, stripping confirmations. Then a senior Advisor said:
The seconds you saved me might let me submit a multi-million-dollar loan without seeing the collateral.
That reframed everything. In finance, some friction is a bug; some is a feature.

items.label: Removed — bug friction
items.desc: Re-entering data, not knowing the next step — removed by conditional logic, inline validation, and guidance.

items.label: Kept & hardened — prudent friction
items.desc: A deliberate, un-skippable confirmation of terms and collateral before submission — kept and hardened, because it carries accountability and risk control.

blocks.value: I demoed both in one prototype — this step fast on purpose, that step slow on purpose — so Product and Compliance saw that efficiency and prudence weren't in conflict, just deliberately separated.

I delivered pixel-perfect handoff across regional variants and product types — SBL, Custom Credit, PLP — with full edge-case and error-state coverage, and stayed in engineering standups through implementation.

indexedSections.title: Proving it worked, with nothing to measure against

value: After launch, my first priority was proving the redesign helped. I hit a wall immediately: v1 had shipped with no success definition — no instrumentation, no baseline. And the hard data I needed, NIGO rate and completion time, was scattered across compliance, ops, and regional systems I couldn't access.

blocks.label: The honest starting point
blocks.value: I had a product I believed was better — and no evidence to prove it. Step one of validation wasn't analysis; it was building the entire practice of validation from scratch.

blocks.title: Never mistake a passed review for validation

value: Reviews are attended by POs and leadership, not the Advisors filling tickets daily. Approved ≠ usable. The real problems hide in edge cases a review room never sees.

So I built my own loop: high-fidelity prototypes made with LLM-assisted tooling, tested with Advisors alongside a UX researcher. One risk needed care — LLM prototypes look so polished that testers "play along" and report false ease. So we never asked "does this feel usable?" We gave real tasks and watched where they stalled, where they reached for the phone.

items.label: Task-based
items.title: Loan Request App
items.desc: Measured completion time and error points on real origination tasks.

items.label: Navigation-based
items.title: Lending Workspace
items.desc: Tested findability: can you find it, and does your mental map match ours

blocks.value: Eleven real Advisors surfaced stall points no one had raised in review.

blocks.label: Key findings — centralization wins but calls persist, risk collaboration belongs in-workflow, high-value features went undiscovered

blocks.title: Translate “the Advisor got stuck” into numbers the bank accepts

value: A tension followed: I had vivid qualitative insight, but the bank's stakeholders trust numbers. "Advisors stall at the collateral step" carried no weight alone.
So I translated qualitative into quantitative, structuring every stall point on three dimensions:

items.label: Frequency
items.title: % of Advisors who hit it
items.desc: How widespread is this stall point across sessions?

items.label: Cost
items.title: Extra time it burns
items.desc: Average minutes lost per occurrence.

items.label: Consequence
items.title: Call-ins it triggers
items.desc: How often it escalates into a phone call for help.

blocks.value: I even structured the soft "Advisors like it" feedback into a trackable satisfaction signal. A UX problem became a problem with frequency, cost, and consequence — and stakeholders could act on it.

value: When completion time dropped, I didn't rush to claim credit — "−30%" is the number that invites "how do you know it was the design?" It could come from process change, training, or sample differences.

So I separated cause from effect. We'd changed many things at once — conditional logic, inline validation, embedded guidance, progressive disclosure — so in validation I mapped which stall point each decision resolved.

items.label: Lagging vs. leading
items.title: Proxy metrics first
items.desc: NIGO only shows up after submissions clear review — so call-ins and first-pass rate read the trend early.

items.label: Comparable data
items.title: One definition, four regions
items.desc: Each market defined "successful submission" differently — I standardized it before comparing anything.

blocks.label: Why the number holds
blocks.value: The resulting −30% holds up under questioning. It isn't a flattering coincidence.

blocks.title: A retro that points to what's next

blocks.label: What a retro is for
blocks.value: The value of a retro isn't proving “I was right.” It's answering “what's next.”

value: Many reviews stop at "metrics hit, project shipped." I turned the findings into roadmap input: which edge cases earn the next iteration, negotiated with engineering and regional POs.

And the testing exposed a bigger opportunity: the real friction isn't only in the Advisor's screens. It lives in the manual back-and-forth with Credit Middle Officers, and in where AI could streamline guidance. One retro started the next body of work.

blocks.label: The Advisor ↔ CMO state map — happy and unhappy paths, where the manual back-and-forth lives

indexedSections.title: Numbers that hold up under questioning

items.label: reduction in ticket completion time
items.desc: Removed bug friction without touching prudent friction.

items.label: Reduced NIGO rate
items.desc: Embedded tooltips and progressive disclosure cut errors and Advisor call-ins.

items.label: Adoption expanded EMEA → USPB
items.desc: One unified skeleton, proved across two major markets.

items.label: Positive Advisor feedback at launch
items.desc: Credited the redesign with reducing friction and improving completion confidence.

blocks.label: Before / after — the v1 flat form vs. Loan Request 3.0

blocks.value: These numbers were believed because they sat on a validation chain I built myself, cause cleanly separated from effect.

blocks.label: The real win
blocks.value: The win wasn't trading prudence for speed. It was replacing wasted friction with necessary friction.

value: I joined by listening first — meeting triad partners, studying existing research, learning the design system — before taking end-to-end ownership.

My biggest takeaway is a decision-making mindset: when a room can't agree in the abstract, the fastest path forward isn't more debate — it's a prototype people can touch, so the solution argues itself.

And the work doesn't end at shipping: a designer has to prove it works, to people who don't trust design. With no baseline and unreachable data, I built the validation loop myself, translated qualitative into quantitative, attributed gains rigorously, and turned a retro into a roadmap.
That, to me, is senior design: crafting the interface, helping conflicting stakeholders decide, knowing which friction to fight and which to defend — and owning every decision with data.
